st.headline: Economists raise Singapore’s 2026 growth forecast to 5% on AI boom: MAS survey
st.teaser: Respondents also raised their predictions for manufacturing and non-oil domestic exports.
fullText: SINGAPORE – Private-sector economists have bumped up their 2026 growth forecast for Singapore’s economy to 5 per cent, up from 3.5 per cent, following a surprise surge in exports and manufacturing output in the first half.

Released on Sept 2, the latest Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) quarterly survey of professional forecasters follows the Ministry of Trade and Industry’s Aug 11 upgrade of its gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast to between 4.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent , up from 2 to 4 per cent , amid the global AI boom.

Enterprise Singapore also on Aug 11 upgraded its non-oil domestic exports (NODX) forecast for 2026 to a range of 14 per cent to 16 per cent, up from an earlier forecast of 3 to 5 per cent , reflecting the exceptionally strong first-half performance led by electronics.
Singapore’s economy grew by 5.9 per cent year on year in the second quarter of 2026 , following a 6.3 per cent expansion in the first quarter.

The respondents in MAS’ latest survey raised their prediction for manufacturing to 8.4 per cent on the back of a 17 per cent surge in Singapore’s NODX amid the strong demand for AI-related electronic hardware such as semiconductors and the machines that make them.
This is a big jump from their June forecast of 5 per cent for manufacturing and 6.1 per cent for NODX.
All economists in the survey identified a sustained AI-driven upturn in the technology cycle as a key support to Singapore’s economic outlook, which could lift GDP growth even higher.
They highlighted that a de-escalation or resolution of the Middle East conflict and stronger-than-expected global growth could deliver possible upside for the economy.

However, the survey also cited downside risks to Singapore’s economic outlook if the now six-month-old Iran war escalates or turns into a more prolonged conflict. It also pointed out Singapore’s vulnerability to a potential burst in the AI bubble and the resulting spillover into financial markets.

The respondents raised their growth forecasts for several sectors: finance and insurance to 5.4 per cent (from 4.5 per cent); construction to 7.1 per cent (from 6.5 per cent); and wholesale and retail trade to 7.4 per cent (from 4.9 per cent).
However, the projection for the accommodation and food services sector was lowered to 1 per cent from the June forecast of 1.8 per cent.
The economists also saw a slightly better inflation outcome.
The latest survey’s median forecast for all-items inflation for 2026 came in at 2.1 per cent, lower than the 2.3 per cent in June.
The median forecast for core inflation – which excludes private transport and accommodation costs to better represent household expenses – was also lowered to 1.9 per cent from 2 per cent.
On the outlook for the labour market, respondents expect the overall unemployment rate to remain at 2.1 per cent at year-end, unchanged from the June 2026 survey.

On monetary policy, 45 per cent of the respondents expected the MAS to tighten – seeking a stronger trade- weighted Singapore dollar – in October by increasing the slope of the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate policy band.
This is higher than the 30 per cent who expected the same move in the previous survey.

cna.headline: UN says world must navigate 'reality' of 1.5°C overshoot
cna.teaser: UN says world must navigate 'reality' of 1.5°C overshoot
fullText: PARIS: The United Nations outlined on Wednesday (Sep 2) how the world might bring global temperatures back to 1.5°C once the milestone target is breached in a first-of-its-kind assessment that drew criticism from climate activists.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres last year acknowledged the inevitability of overshooting 1.5°C, but this is the first time a UN agency has addressed this head-on in a dedicated report.
Scientists agree that warming above 1.5°C relative to pre-industrial times poses grave risks and nearly 200 nations committed in 2015 to try and keep global temperature rises to this safer threshold.
But the world is expected to blow past 1.5°C in a matter of years and attention has pivoted to making any "overshoot" as brief and contained as possible.
"It's a reality check. We have to live with this warmer world ... but there's still a lot we can do to limit warming," said report co-author Richard Betts from the University of Exeter.
The report "was about responses rather than just sort of saying it is happening", he told journalists.
Fellow author Debra Roberts said it was important for policymakers "to realise the rules of the game are now changing".

"I think for me that's the clarion call ... we now have to reconfigure our climate governance around dealing with an overshoot pathway. None of our plans are prepared for that," said Roberts from the University of KwaZulu-Natal.
The report's stark language alarmed climate campaigners who have rallied around 1.5°C since it was affirmed as the more ambitious goal of the Paris Agreement a decade ago.
"This is a heartbreaking moment, but overshoot is not the reason to give up and surrender 1.5°C", said Jasper Inventor, Deputy Programme Director at Greenpeace International.
Bill Hare, a climate scientist and CEO of policy institute Climate Analytics, slammed the report and said it risked becoming "a call to apathy rather than a call to arms".

Small island nations threatened by rising seas have been particularly vocal defenders of the 1.5°C target and have urged wealthier countries not to abandon the milestone even as it slips out of reach.
The world has already warmed roughly 1.4°C since the 1850s to 1900s, mostly from the burning of fossil fuels, and the last three years have been the hottest on record .
Scientists say any overshoot of 1.5°C threatens more extreme weather and pushes the planet closer to tipping points like the collapse of ice sheets and loss of coral reefs.
UNEP executive director Inger Andersen said there "are no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C".
"Let's be very clear - that 1.5°C target is still the goal. But now, we need to approach it differently: from above," Andersen told journalists.
Guterres said it was possible to bring warming back below 1.5°C by the end of the century.
"The fight for 1.5 degrees is the fight for humanity," he said.

To achieve this, carbon dioxide removal - the process of pulling carbon from the air and storing it - would be essential alongside deep and rapid cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, the UNEP report said.
At present, carbon removal plays a vanishingly small part in addressing climate change and is strongly opposed by many activists pushing for a faster phase-out of coal, oil and gas.
"The only way to minimise harm is to cut emissions now ... not to delay action with speculative techno-fixes," said Lili Fuhr from campaign organisation CIEL.

listening.title: Singapore's Wet Markets Embrace Digital Payments
listening.transcript: As Singapore marches towards a cashless society, local wet market stallholders are increasingly adopting e-payment systems like SGQR. Initially, elderly vendors were hesitant to abandon cash transactions, citing concerns over technology. However, targeted government grants and community digital ambassadors have successfully eased this transition, keeping traditional businesses viable in a digital economy.

economistArticle.title: Europe’s bond markets are suffering a post-holiday shock
paras: As European traders returned from their summer vacations, they were greeted by an unsettling reality. The continent's sovereign bond markets, traditionally seen as a haven of stability, have suffered a sharp post-holiday shock. Yields on benchmark German Bunds and French OATs have surged to levels not seen in months, triggering anxieties across eurozone boardrooms and policy circles. Unlike previous market tantrums, this sudden sell-off cannot be dismissed as a mere seasonal blip.

The drivers behind this European fixed-income rout differ subtly but significantly from those driving yields up in the United States. In Washington, Treasury yields have risen on the back of resilient economic growth and fears that the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates elevated to curb sticky inflation. Europe, by contrast, is staring down the barrel of economic stagnation. The Eurozone's spike in yields is not a reflection of economic vitality, but rather a manifestation of compounding fiscal anxieties and fears of structural decay.

Foremost among these concerns is the European Central Bank’s aggressive quantitative tightening. As the central bank shrinks its balance sheet, the safety net that once suppressed southern European debt yields is rapidly dissolving. Highly indebted nations, particularly Italy, are finding themselves exposed to the harsh elements of market discipline. The premium investors demand to hold Italian debt over German benchmarks has widened precariously, raising the specter of past sovereign debt crises.

Compounding this pressure is a deluge of new government debt. European nations are borrowing heavily to finance green energy transitions, bolster defense spending in the wake of geopolitical tensions, and shield consumers from high living costs. With the central bank no longer acting as the buyer of last resort, private investors must absorb this massive supply. To attract these buyers, governments are forced to offer increasingly lucrative yields, which in turn drives up borrowing costs for businesses and homeowners alike.

The ramifications of this post-holiday shock are profound. Higher yields mean that the cost of servicing public debt will devour an increasing share of national budgets, forcing painful fiscal choices. For a continent already struggling with sluggish productivity and political polarization, a prolonged period of elevated borrowing costs could choke off what little economic momentum remains, turning a cyclical slowdown into a structural freeze.
economistArticle.cn:
随着欧洲交易员结束夏日假期重返岗位，他们迎来了令人不安的现实。传统上被视为避风港的欧洲国债市场遭遇了剧烈的“节后休克”。作为基准的德国联邦国债和法国国债收益率已飙升至数月未见的水平，引发了整个欧元区董事会和政策圈的焦虑。与以往的市场动荡不同，这次突如其来的抛售不能仅仅被视为季节性的短暂波动。

欧洲固定收益市场此番溃败的幕后推手，与推高美国国债收益率的因素存在微妙但显著的差异。在华盛顿，美债收益率上升是由于经济增长具有韧性，以及市场担忧美联储将维持高利率以遏制顽固的通胀。相比之下，欧洲正面临经济停滞的困境。欧元区收益率的飙升并非经济活力的体现，而是财政焦虑加剧和对结构性衰退担忧的具体表露。

在这些担忧中，首当其冲的是欧洲中央银行（ECB）激进的量化紧缩政策。随着央行缩减资产负债表，曾一度压低南欧债务收益率的安全网正在迅速瓦解。高负债国家，尤其是意大利，发现自己正暴露在残酷的市场规律之下。投资者持有意大利国债而非德国基准国债所要求的溢价（即备受关注的BTP-Bund利差）已危险地扩大，引发了人们对过去主权债务危机的担忧。

加剧这一压力的还有汹涌而至的新增政府债务。面对地缘政治紧张局势，欧洲国家正大量借债，以资助绿色能源转型、加强国防开支，并保护消费者免受高生活成本的影响。由于欧洲央行不再充当最后的买家，私人投资者必须消化这一庞大的供应。为了吸引这些买家，各国政府被迫提供越来越有吸引力的收益率，这反过来又推高了企业和购房者的借贷成本。

这场节后休克的影响是深远的。更高的收益率意味着偿还公共债务的成本将吞噬日益增加的国家预算份额，从而迫使政府做出痛苦的财政选择。对于一个已经与生产力低下和政治极分化作斗争的大陆来说，借贷成本长期处于高位可能会扼杀仅存的经济势头，将周期性放缓变成结构性停滞。

gems.s: Unlike previous market tantrums, this sudden sell-off cannot be dismissed as a mere seasonal blip.
gems.why: This sentence uses a contrasting subordinate clause and sophisticated vocabulary like 'tantrums' and 'seasonal blip' to establish gravity. 它使用对比从句和高级词汇（如tantrums, seasonal blip）来确立事态的严重性。

gems.s: The Eurozone's spike in yields is not a reflection of economic vitality, but rather a manifestation of compounding fiscal anxieties and fears of structural decay.
gems.why: The use of the 'not... but rather...' structure creates a powerful contrast that sharpens the analytical tone of the argument. “not... but rather...”结构创造了强烈的对比，使论点的分析性语气更为鲜明。
